Trump and the MAGA enthusiasm strategy

TRUMP AND THE MAGA ENTHUSIASM STRATEGY. Actual Article Body:
TRUMP AND THE MAGA ENTHUSIASM STRATEGY. In a conversation on board Air Force One, bound for Sioux City, Iowa, and another midterm rally for Republican candidates, I asked President Donald Trump whether, despite the excitement he sees at his rallies, he thinks the GOP is going to lose the House. Instead of answering immediately, he asked what I thought. I said yes, I think the GOP is going to lose. But I hoped to hear his view on the widespread belief that House Republicans are headed for defeat.

“People say that,” Trump said. “I just don’t see it. There’s such enthusiasm. You’ll see, you’ll go there today.”

Indeed, the Sioux City rally, held at the airport, was raucous; the crowd was clearly stoked. Then the president pointed to several of his other rallies. “You saw last night?” he said, referring to a wildly enthusiastic rally in South Carolina. And then he mentioned his much-talked-about Oct. 13 trip to Alaska.

“I took him from losing to being ahead,” Trump said of Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is fighting for reelection not only against a strong bid from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola but also against what is essentially a Democratic dirty trick by a man named “Dan Sullivan” who registered as a Republican to run in hopes of pulling votes away from the real Sen. Sullivan. Trump couldn’t believe that on the Alaska ballot the real and the fake Dan Sullivan appeared indistinguishable.

As we discussed how Republicans can win, Trump pointed to GOP redistricting efforts to flip some Democratic seats. “We have the advantage of picking up some seats, right?” he said. He then asked “How many?” I said five, or maybe 10. Trump responded with “Eight? Nine?” All those numbers, including mine, were a little higher than some recent predictions that the GOP redistricting work will backfire, and Republicans will pick up seats in the low single digits. But who knows?

“I might be wrong,” Trump told me. “The country’s never done better. People feel good. The gasoline’s a little high, but it’s coming down. You know, gasoline is lower than it was with Biden and Obama, and I got rid of the nuclear threat.”

Trump’s critics will scoff at his “never done better” claim, and at least some of his supporters might wince. Indeed, one could make the alternative argument that Trump was elected to do one big thing — bring down inflation — and inflation on a yearly basis was 3% when Trump took office in January 2025, and it is 3.7% today. That’s nowhere near where it was — 9.1% — in the worst of the Joe Biden years, but Trump promised it would go down, and it hasn’t.

On the other hand, there is the bill of particulars Trump offered voters in Sioux City and every other place he has held rallies. Look at the stock market, he told the crowd in Iowa, and look at your 401(k). They’re both up. Then: “Income for hardworking Americans has soared to the highest level ever recorded.” That’s true. And then: “The poverty rate has just reached its best level in American history.” That’s true, too, referring to the period in which the rate has been recorded. Then Trump cited other improvements, in manufacturing and exports, some of which were overstated but did indeed reflect progress under Trump. In addition, for Iowa specifically, on Sept. 30 Trump announced the planned construction of a huge new steel plant in the state, which outgoing Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds called “transformational.”

“You just heard six statistics,” Trump told the crowd, resting his case. “Ladies and gentlemen, goodnight. I love Iowa very much. I’m leaving. How the hell can I beat it?” Trump jokingly started to walk offstage, his work done, while the audience cheered.

Say what you want, but that’s not nothing. At his rallies, Trump presents a compelling case for solid economic accomplishments — to go along with the higher energy and food prices that have made inflation so stubborn in the months after Trump started the war in Iran. He promises, of course, that gas prices will plunge as soon as the war ends, which he thinks will be after the midterm elections. That will be great if it happens, although until then prices will remain a real problem. Still, the good indicators in the economy are real.

So are Trump’s tax cuts. Onstage in Sioux City, he polled the crowd on their opinion of his moves to eliminate taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security. Reflecting the area’s economic and demographic makeup, no tax on tips was somewhat popular; no tax on overtime was more popular; and no tax on Social Security was really, really popular.

All of this, good and bad, factors into Trump’s job approval rating, which stands at 38.8% approval and 60.4% disapproval, according to the RealClearPolitics average of polls. A president’s job approval rating is one of the best predictors of his party’s midterm results, and Trump’s is, for Republicans, dangerously low.

I asked him about the job approval number. “It’s fake,” he quickly said. “It’s fake.” He pointed to the New York Times’s use of phony “Wedgewood” polls. That was a moment of real embarrassment for the paper, even though the New York Times said it did not use “Wedgewood” polls in calculating the president’s job approval rating. Nevertheless, Trump made the fake poll part of a larger indictment of polling. “The job approval, they said it’s 37, 38?” he asked incredulously. “I’m not at 38.”

I asked where he thought his approval rating actually stands. “I don’t believe I could be beaten by anybody,” Trump said. “I think that if I needed it, which I don’t, I think 60.”

What does that mean? Trump would say it means what he says — that his real job approval rating is 60%. I asked if he meant that he would be at 60 if he were running for office himself. “Yeah, I think I’d be in the 60s now,” he said. “Now, in the Republican Party, I’m way up. Show him the 99%. Have you seen it?”

By that last part, Trump was asking an aide to show me a video clip that he is fond of playing, of CNN’s Harry Enten, from Sept. 27, in which Enten said, “In the 2024 election versus Kamala Harris, [Trump] got 99% of the MAGA GOP vote. Perhaps surprisingly, I might have thought it would be 100%, but it was 99%. Compare that to his approval rating now with the MAGA GOP. It’s 98%.”

Put those numbers together with Trump’s experiences at his rallies, where he addresses large, enthusiastic crowds, and then add to that the persuasive fact that he has twice been elected president of the United States — add that all together and it accounts for Trump’s belief in his own popularity and ability to influence elections, even those in which he is not running.

I asked, “Do you ever think that you get such big, adoring crowds, and it’s almost like a bubble? Do you think, These 10,000 people, man, they love me, but the larger electorate, I’ve got to win their votes. I mean, there are independents out there?”

“I always cater to my base,” Trump said. “My base is big. I think my base is close to 100% of the Republican Party. … I think I’m close to 100. … It’s not MAGA, it’s just —.” At that moment, I interjected, “But it’s not the whole Republican Party.” Trump answered: “I think it’s close. I think the Bushes have largely faded. They’re gone.”

That’s certainly true. But the bottom line is that Trump sometimes views his Republican base as if it is the electorate as a whole. He draws impressive crowds made up of supporters who love him. He spends much of his time among people who revere him. Viewed from that perspective, a job approval rating of 38.8% just doesn’t make any sense.

If you start with Trump’s belief that economic indicators are strong for coming growth, and add his skepticism of polls, and then throw in his confidence in his sky-high, rock-solid approval ratings among his MAGA base — together, they add up to Trump’s belief that Republicans can win not just the Senate, which many observers see as too close to call right now, but the House, too, which those observers believe is lost to the GOP.

Trump knows the polls, of course. He is a close and discriminating reader of news stories. And he has certainly heard advisers, consultants, and others describe the adverse conditions Republicans face in races across the country. But what should he do? Tell his party that they’re going to lose? Trump knows how many Republicans look to him for leadership. If he appears to lose hope, they will, too. So he keeps at it as he nears the end of an extraordinary 32-day cross-country campaign tour. And he has a case to make.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., lashed out at President Donald Trump on Friday after he accused her of using a fake name and revived longstanding allegations surrounding her former marriage.

"The pedophile protection party's president is laundering right-wing conspiracy theories through the most corrupt DOJ in American history," Omar wrote on X.

A Justice Department court filing this week, related to a search warrant for her Washington-area home, identified the Minnesota Democrat as "Congresswoman Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar."

Omar's office disputed Fox News Digital's reporting, insisting, "Ilhan Omar is her real name." Omar has not been charged with a crime.

"It was just revealed that Ilhan Omar's name is not Ilhan Omar," Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday, accusing the congresswoman of using a "fake name" and calling for her immediate resignation. Trump also revived longstanding allegations that Omar's former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, is her brother — claims Omar has repeatedly denied. He pointed out that the name used in the DOJ filings matched that of the man she allegedly married and is related to.

When asked during an MS NOW interview this week whether there was any familial relationship with Elmi, Omar responded, "Not to my knowledge." Her spokesperson later said the answer was sarcastic and reiterated that Omar "repeatedly and unequivocally" denied the allegation.

Rep. Ilhan Omar eats lunch in Karmel Mall of Somalia in Minneapolis. Minn.. Friday, October 23, 2026. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

Federal investigators are probing whether Omar or her father made false statements on immigration paperwork.

Agents searched Omar's Washington, D.C., residence earlier this month and seized her cellphone and passport, while her sister has also been questioned as part of the investigation, Fox News Digital previously reported.

Fox News Digital's Peter D'Abrosca and Pedro Rodriguez-Aparicio contributed to this report.

Trump Threatens Iran Strike — ‘We May Do Another Little Epic Fury’

President Donald Trump warned Friday that the United States could launch another round of military strikes against Iran unless Tehran reaches an agreement, escalating his threats as Washington intensifies economic pressure on the Islamic Republic.
The post Trump Threatens Iran Strike — ‘We May Do Another Little Epic Fury’ appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
President Donald Trump warned Friday that the United States could launch another round of military strikes against Iran unless Tehran reaches an agreement, escalating his threats as Washington intensifies economic pressure on the Islamic Republic.

“We may do another little Epic Fury, or they’ll agree,” Trump told supporters at a midterm campaign rally in Fort Myers, Florida, referring to the U.S. military operation launched against Iran in February.

“If they’re smart, they’ll just say, ‘Let’s get down to business.’ But, you know, I doubt they’ll do that because perhaps they’re not smart,” he added.

The remarks marked Trump’s latest warning of renewed military action against Tehran, following his declaration Thursday that American forces had already “knocked the hell out of” Iran and might go “a little bit further.”

Earlier Friday, Trump asserted that the United States controlled the Strait of Hormuz, allowing other countries to ship oil through the strategic waterway while restricting Iran’s own exports.

“The question is, do we want to finish it off, or do we just want to let it wither? Because we’re getting everything we want,” Trump told reporters.

He went further in a separate exchange, suggesting that the United States possessed the military capability to seize Iran’s oil resources or even the country itself.

“We could take the whole country. We could take all of the oil,” he said. “And as you know, the Hormuz Strait is totally ours, and that’s the way we’ll keep it.”

The president’s remarks came as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared that American efforts to isolate Iran economically had devastated its oil-export network while allowing energy shipments from the wider Persian Gulf to recover.

“Despite Iran’s efforts to disrupt energy shipments, oil exports from the Persian Gulf are roaring back and have surpassed pre-conflict levels,” Bessent wrote Friday.

“The message is clear: Iran’s threats have failed to stop the flow of energy to global markets,” he added.

In a separate statement earlier Friday, Bessent credited the administration’s Operation Economic Outcast with depleting Iran’s shadow tanker fleet, emptying its main oil terminal and exhausting its offshore reserves.

“As President Trump takes action that his predecessors long deferred, the United States is no longer managing the Iranian threat. We are ending it,” he declared.

Trump’s remarks also reflected the competing approaches to Iran detailed in a Thursday report by The Atlantic, which described Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent advocating sustained economic pressure while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has urged Trump to pursue another round of devastating strikes aimed at toppling the Iranian regime.

According to the report, the Trump administration is considering combining the two strategies, potentially launching several days of strikes after the November midterm elections against Iranian missile and drone capabilities, energy infrastructure and nuclear facilities. An outside adviser cited in the report argued that economic pressure had brought Iran close to collapse and that additional strikes “would push them over.”

The prospect of more immediate military action surfaced Friday when U.S. Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack suggested that American forces could strike Iran as soon as this weekend.

“Could there be a strike this weekend? Absolutely,” Barrack said during an interview with Mario Nawfal, while emphasizing that Trump remained open to a negotiated agreement.

Asked about Barrack’s remarks before his Florida rally, Trump appeared to playfully question the ambassador’s authority to predict military action.

“That’s my ambassador to Turkey. He’s a pretty powerful man, I guess,” Trump quipped.

“If that’s the case, I don’t know anything about it,” he added.

The president appeared to dismiss Barrack’s suggestion of an imminent strike without ruling out further military action.

Meanwhile, Iran has warned of retaliation if Washington resumes its military campaign.

Reuters reported Friday that two senior Iranian security officials described contingency plans to attack undersea communications cables in the Persian Gulf, including efforts to prevent repairs and prolong disruptions.

“If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines … from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones,” one official warned.

Separately, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Brig. Gen. Yadollah Javani threatened that Iran would become a killing ground for foreign troops if the United States attempted a ground invasion.

The escalating warnings come as Washington moves diplomatic personnel and family members out of several Middle Eastern countries. CNN reported Friday that the State Department had quietly adjusted staffing at embassies in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Lebanon, in addition to ordering the departure of non-emergency personnel and family members from Saudi Arabia amid intensified attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthis.

Despite the heightened tensions, the administration continues to insist that a diplomatic agreement remains possible.

U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz said Friday that the American blockade could be maintained for the foreseeable future and that Washington’s pressure campaign was intensifying, while emphasizing that decisions about the duration of the confrontation and any further military action ultimately rest with Trump.

“The president and the U.S. Navy can maintain this blockade for their foreseeable future. The maximum pressure campaign is only tightening,” Waltz said.

Joshua Klein is a reporter for Breitbart News. Email him at jklein@breitbart.com. Follow him on Twitter @JoshuaKlein.

If you start with Trump’s belief that economic indicators are strong for coming growth, and add his skepticism of polls, and then throw in his confidence in his sky-high, rock-solid approval ratings among his MAGA base — together, they add up to Trump’s belief that Republicans can win not just the Senate, which many observers see as too close to call right now, but the House, too, which those observers believe is lost to the GOP.

Trump knows the polls, of course. He is a close and discriminating reader of news stories. And he has certainly heard advisers, consultants, and others describe the adverse conditions Republicans face in races across the country. But what should he do? Tell his party that they’re going to lose? Trump knows how many Republicans look to him for leadership. If he appears to lose hope, they will, too. So he keeps at it as he nears the end of an extraordinary 32-day cross-country campaign tour. And he has a case to make.

Trump Threatens Iran Strike — ‘We May Do Another Little Epic Fury’

President Donald Trump warned Friday that the United States could launch another round of military strikes against Iran unless Tehran reaches an agreement, escalating his threats as Washington intensifies economic pressure on the Islamic Republic.
The post Trump Threatens Iran Strike — ‘We May Do Another Little Epic Fury’ appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
President Donald Trump warned Friday that the United States could launch another round of military strikes against Iran unless Tehran reaches an agreement, escalating his threats as Washington intensifies economic pressure on the Islamic Republic.

“We may do another little Epic Fury, or they’ll agree,” Trump told supporters at a midterm campaign rally in Fort Myers, Florida, referring to the U.S. military operation launched against Iran in February.

“If they’re smart, they’ll just say, ‘Let’s get down to business.’ But, you know, I doubt they’ll do that because perhaps they’re not smart,” he added.

The remarks marked Trump’s latest warning of renewed military action against Tehran, following his declaration Thursday that American forces had already “knocked the hell out of” Iran and might go “a little bit further.”

Earlier Friday, Trump asserted that the United States controlled the Strait of Hormuz, allowing other countries to ship oil through the strategic waterway while restricting Iran’s own exports.

“The question is, do we want to finish it off, or do we just want to let it wither? Because we’re getting everything we want,” Trump told reporters.

He went further in a separate exchange, suggesting that the United States possessed the military capability to seize Iran’s oil resources or even the country itself.

“We could take the whole country. We could take all of the oil,” he said. “And as you know, the Hormuz Strait is totally ours, and that’s the way we’ll keep it.”

The president’s remarks came as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared that American efforts to isolate Iran economically had devastated its oil-export network while allowing energy shipments from the wider Persian Gulf to recover.

“Despite Iran’s efforts to disrupt energy shipments, oil exports from the Persian Gulf are roaring back and have surpassed pre-conflict levels,” Bessent wrote Friday.

“The message is clear: Iran’s threats have failed to stop the flow of energy to global markets,” he added.

In a separate statement earlier Friday, Bessent credited the administration’s Operation Economic Outcast with depleting Iran’s shadow tanker fleet, emptying its main oil terminal and exhausting its offshore reserves.

“As President Trump takes action that his predecessors long deferred, the United States is no longer managing the Iranian threat. We are ending it,” he declared.

Trump’s remarks also reflected the competing approaches to Iran detailed in a Thursday report by The Atlantic, which described Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent advocating sustained economic pressure while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has urged Trump to pursue another round of devastating strikes aimed at toppling the Iranian regime.

According to the report, the Trump administration is considering combining the two strategies, potentially launching several days of strikes after the November midterm elections against Iranian missile and drone capabilities, energy infrastructure and nuclear facilities. An outside adviser cited in the report argued that economic pressure had brought Iran close to collapse and that additional strikes “would push them over.”

The prospect of more immediate military action surfaced Friday when U.S. Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack suggested that American forces could strike Iran as soon as this weekend.

“Could there be a strike this weekend? Absolutely,” Barrack said during an interview with Mario Nawfal, while emphasizing that Trump remained open to a negotiated agreement.

Asked about Barrack’s remarks before his Florida rally, Trump appeared to playfully question the ambassador’s authority to predict military action.

“That’s my ambassador to Turkey. He’s a pretty powerful man, I guess,” Trump quipped.

“If that’s the case, I don’t know anything about it,” he added.

The president appeared to dismiss Barrack’s suggestion of an imminent strike without ruling out further military action.

Meanwhile, Iran has warned of retaliation if Washington resumes its military campaign.

Reuters reported Friday that two senior Iranian security officials described contingency plans to attack undersea communications cables in the Persian Gulf, including efforts to prevent repairs and prolong disruptions.

“If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines … from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones,” one official warned.

Separately, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Brig. Gen. Yadollah Javani threatened that Iran would become a killing ground for foreign troops if the United States attempted a ground invasion.

The escalating warnings come as Washington moves diplomatic personnel and family members out of several Middle Eastern countries. CNN reported Friday that the State Department had quietly adjusted staffing at embassies in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Lebanon, in addition to ordering the departure of non-emergency personnel and family members from Saudi Arabia amid intensified attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthis.

Despite the heightened tensions, the administration continues to insist that a diplomatic agreement remains possible.

U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz said Friday that the American blockade could be maintained for the foreseeable future and that Washington’s pressure campaign was intensifying, while emphasizing that decisions about the duration of the confrontation and any further military action ultimately rest with Trump.

“The president and the U.S. Navy can maintain this blockade for their foreseeable future. The maximum pressure campaign is only tightening,” Waltz said.
